abstract: Centrin is a conserved protein that localizes to centrioles and basal bodies across eukaryotes, where it performs scaffolding and structural functions. In ciliates, centrin additionally assembles into patterned, cellular-scale networks required for ultrafast changes in cell shape. Across distantly related algae, centrin forms fibrillar structures that connect the basal bodies to one another and to the nucleus. These features suggest that centrin has cytoskeletal functions, generating and resisting mechanical forces, yet its functions in this context remain poorly understood. Here, we use expansion microscopy and centrin mutants with different network morphologies to study the function of centrin filaments in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. Consistent with previous studies, centrin localizes to the basal bodies and transition zones, to the distal striated fiber, which connects the distal ends of the two basal bodies, and to filaments that extend from the basal bodies toward the nucleus, where they branch into a network that surrounds it. Using mutants of basal body proteins, we show that these centrin fibers assemble independently of basal bodies, which anchor and orient them. Centrin mutants have shorter cilia that regenerate more slowly, consistent with centrin's structural roles at the basal bodies and transition zones. Beyond these structural roles, centrin serves a mechanical function at the distal striated fiber. Mutants with structural defects in this centrin network show altered ciliary beat frequency and lack synchrony between the two cilia, resulting in impaired swimming. Moreover, the transition zone, the distal striated fiber, and the nucleus-basal body connectors each contract in response to calcium. Together, these results show that centrin assembles into basal body-associated networks that combine structural scaffolding with calcium-responsive contractility and force transmission. Our findings establish centrin as a bona fide cytoskeletal protein and provide insight into how a single protein can diversify to perform distinct structural and mechanical functions within the same cell.
